name: Kilindi Zanzibar
neighborhood: Kendwa · the north end, in 50 acres of garden

why: The strangest building on this coast and the best argument for walking north out of Kendwa village. Fifteen white domed pavilions stand in fifty acres of tropical garden — the original commission was a private house for Benny Andersson of ABBA, and the domes, the glassless windows and the roofless rain showers are all his architect's, not a hotel group's. Elewana (Minor Hotels) runs it now: butler per pavilion, waterfall bar, dinner laid al fresco or on the sand. It is not a restaurant you drop into — it is a room you go and stay in, and the cooking is confident resort European-Swahili, not a destination kitchen. Go for the architecture and the silence.

name: Nungwi fish market & the evening grills
neighborhood: Nungwi · the working beach, north of the hotel line
hours: Boats and auction from first light; the charcoal grills fire up from about 18:00 until the fish runs out
why: The single most useful address in this guide and the cheapest. In the morning it is a landing and an auction — kingfish, tuna, snapper, octopus and squid coming off the ngalawa and the mashua, sold by shouted bid on the sand. By evening the same ground turns into the village's own restaurant: vendors light charcoal, you point at what you want from the ice, it is weighed, grilled and handed over with rice, salad and a chilli-lime sauce. Local families and off-shift fishermen eat here, which is the only endorsement that has ever mattered. Bring shillings, agree the price per kilo before it goes on the fire, and eat standing up.
hook: An auction at dawn and the village's own grill at dusk, on the same square of sand.
person: The Nungwi boat crews and the grill vendors
signature: A whole reef fish, weighed off the ice and grilled to order, with rice and kachumbari
verdict: The best value and the truest plate on the north tip — and the one place here where the tourist and the fisherman are eating the same fish at the same fire.
caveat: Cash only, no menu, no receipt, and prices are negotiated: settle the price per kilogram before the fish is put on the coals or you will pay a stranger's rate. Hygiene is a working beach's hygiene — go when it is busy and the turnover is fast.
price_range: A few thousand TZS a head to eat well — the cheapest good meal on this coast

name: Zanzibar Watersports @ Kendwa Rocks
neighborhood: Kendwa · on the beach at Kendwa Rocks
hours: Daily, dawn departures for the deep sites
why: The dive and water-sports centre on Kendwa sand, running the full PADI ladder from Discover Scuba to instructor. The sites that matter from here: Leven Bank and the Big Wall for experienced divers, and the shallower Tumbatu and Wattabomi reefs for everyone else.
hook: The Kendwa dive desk — Leven Bank when the tide allows, Tumbatu when it does not.
verdict: The convenient option if you are staying in Kendwa; the deep-site briefing is the thing to listen to.
caveat: Leven Bank is a strong-current, experienced-divers-only site and can only be dived on certain tides. Do not book it as your first dive of a trip.
price_range: Standard Zanzibar dive rates; Mnemba carries a US$10 per-person conservation fee
hot_this_month: Visibility at its annual peak and pelagics on Leven Bank while the kusi runs — ask which tide suits the bank.

name: Spanish Dancer Divers
neighborhood: Nungwi · on the beach
why: Nungwi's longest-running dive centre — a PADI 5-star resort operating since 2001, teaching in English, Spanish, German and French, and running daily to Mnemba Atoll, Leven Bank, Tumbatu and Magic Reef. The institutional memory here is the asset: twenty-five years of watching this water is what tells you which tide to dive.
hook: Diving this water since 2001, in four languages.
verdict: The most experienced dive operation on the north tip, and the one to ask about conditions before you commit.
caveat: Mnemba trips carry the conservation-area fee on top of the dive price.
price_range: Standard rates + US$10 Mnemba conservation fee
hot_this_month: Humpbacks peaking Aug–Sep in the bay and the channel — book the whale trip through the dive desk, not a beach tout.

name: Diving Poseidon
neighborhood: Nungwi · on the beach
why: The third of the north tip's established dive desks, working the same northern sites. Worth a quote if the other two are full on the day you want a specific tide.
hook: The third desk — useful when the tide you want is booked out elsewhere.
verdict: Competent and conveniently placed; compare the briefing, not the price.
caveat: Confirm the boat and the group size before paying.

name: The Nungwi dhow yards
neighborhood: Nungwi · the working beach north of the hotels
hours: Daylight, most days — it is a workplace, not an attraction with hours
why: The north coast is Zanzibar's dhow-building capital and this is where it happens: hulls going up on the open sand, shaped by hand with an adze, planks bent with fire and water, no plans on paper. The little double-outrigger ngalawa is dug from a single mango trunk — a cultivated fruit tree, not forest timber, and a hardwood that holds up in salt water for years. A big jahazi takes months. Nobody here is performing for you; if you watch, watch properly, ask before you photograph a man's hands, and buy a coffee from the vendor at the top of the beach.
address: Nungwi beach, north of the hotel line
hook: Hulls going up on the open sand, shaped by adze and fire, with no drawing anywhere.
signature: Watching a ngalawa hull being dug from a single mango trunk
verdict: The most alive craft on this island and the reason to walk north out of the bar strip at all.
caveat: This is a workplace. Ask before photographing; do not climb on the boats; tip the guide if you take one.
price_range: Free to watch; a guide expects a tip

name: Mnarani Marine Turtles Conservation Pond
neighborhood: Nungwi · by the lighthouse, north-east of the village
why: A natural tidal pool in the coral rag behind the beach, separated from the ocean by a few metres of old reef and flushed by the tide — established in 1993 by local villagers to rescue and rehabilitate green and hawksbill turtles caught in fishing nets. 'Mnarani' means 'at the lighthouse', and the lighthouse is right there. There are separate pools for hatchlings, juveniles and injured animals, a pier and an information pavilion, and every February a public release of the rehabilitated turtles. Of the two turtle attractions on this cape, this is the one with a conservation record rather than a conservation claim.
hook: A tidal pool in the coral rag, run by the village since 1993, with a release every February.
person: Founded 1993 by Nungwi villagers and conservationists
signature: The February release — rehabilitated turtles going back through the surf
verdict: The honest option of the two turtle ponds here: community-founded, tidally flushed, with an actual annual release rather than a website paragraph.
caveat: It is still a captive pond with paying visitors, and the animals are handled. If that is a line for you, do not go — watch for turtles on a Mnemba dive instead.
hot_this_month: Nothing on until the February release — the turtles are here year-round, the event is not.

name: Baraka Natural Aquarium
neighborhood: Nungwi · Mkunguni
why: Listed here because you will be offered it a dozen times and should know what the argument is. The facility's own site states its mission as rescue, rehabilitation and protection, and says it releases animals 'back to the wild where they belong'; swimming with the turtles, feeding them and the zoo are US$10 each. Visitor accounts dispute the picture in strong terms — that the animals are handled and ridden, that the pond is small and crowded, that turtles are bought from fishermen, and that no evidence of releases was produced when asked. We could not resolve the two accounts from here, so we are not going to tell you it is fine.
hook: The contested one — its own site claims releases; a lot of visitors say otherwise.
verdict: Contested, and we could not settle it. If you want turtles, go to Mnarani, or dive Mnemba and see them wild.
caveat: ⚠ Animal-welfare concerns are substantial and repeated in visitor accounts. Read them before you buy a ticket.

name: Ras Nungwi Lighthouse
neighborhood: Nungwi · the northern point itself
hours: Exterior only — it is an operating aid to navigation, not a museum
why: The oldest lighthouse on Unguja, standing on the island's northern point. The station dates to the 1880s and the tower you see — a white three-stage square stone tower with a red lantern — was built in 1926: 14 metres tall, focal height 18 metres, range 13 nautical miles. Sources differ on the first date, 1881 or 1886; we have not been able to settle it, so both are given. This is the light every dhow rounding the cape has steered by for a century.
hook: A century of dhows have rounded this cape on a 13-mile light.
signature: Standing at the point at dusk as the light comes on
verdict: Five minutes of your day and the best orientation on the whole cape — everything in this guide is arranged around this corner.
caveat: No public access to the tower. Sources disagree on whether the first station was 1881 or 1886.

name: Kendwa Beach
neighborhood: Kendwa · the whole west-facing sand
why: The reason this village exists as a destination. Almost everywhere else on Unguja the sea walks out at low water — on the east coast the reef sits a kilometre or more offshore and the flats dry to a moonscape twice a day. Kendwa shelves steeply within metres of the sand, so the water is there whatever the moon is doing. Add a north-west aspect and you have the one beach on this island that is both swimmable all day and pointed at the sunset.
hook: The one beach on Unguja that keeps its water at low tide — and faces the sunset.
signature: A swim at low water, which almost nowhere else on this island allows
verdict: Not a matter of taste: this is a bathymetric fact and it is why you are here rather than at Paje.
caveat: Public beach — the hawker traffic is constant, and it is a Muslim island: cover up walking off the sand.
best_time: Low water in the late afternoon

name: Mkokotoni landing & market
neighborhood: West coast · the district capital, ~20 km south of Kendwa
hours: Auctions from early morning; the market runs through the morning
why: The real fish market of the north — the district capital's landing, supplying the fish shops in town, and the place to go if the Nungwi market feels like it has learned to price for visitors. Boats come in on the tide, the auction is shouted, and it is over by mid-morning; for the big or unusual fish you have to be there before the first sale. It is also the crossing point for Tumbatu, which sits directly offshore.
hook: The district's real fish auction — and the jetty Tumbatu is reached from.
signature: The first auction of the morning, before the town buyers clear the slab
verdict: If you cook, this is the most useful hour on the island: it is where the north's fish is actually priced.
caveat: Arrive before mid-morning or the good fish is gone. Cash only. This is a working market, not a tour stop.
price_range: Wholesale — bring shillings and small notes

hot_this_month: Spring tides around the 28 Aug full moon — the biggest landings of the month.

name: Tumbatu Island
neighborhood: Offshore, west · the island Kendwa looks at
hours: Daylight crossings from Mkokotoni; permitted visits only
why: The island on your horizon, and the most serious place in this guide. Tumbatu is the third largest island of the archipelago, about eight kilometres long, and its people — the Watumbatu — speak their own dialect of Swahili and trace their descent to Shirazi arrivals. Between roughly 1100 and 1300 it was a state centre trading across the Indian Ocean; Jongowe was among the largest settlements on the whole Zanzibar coast in the 1150s–1250s, and the ruins of a Shirazi mosque of the eleventh or twelfth century stand in the forest at Makutani. The Watumbatu are also, by long reputation, the best sailors on Zanzibar and arguably on the East African coast.
hook: A medieval city-state on your horizon, whose people are still the best sailors on this coast.
signature: The Shirazi mosque ruins in the forest at Makutani
verdict: The most historically important thing visible from Kendwa sand, and the one you are least entitled to walk into.
caveat: ⚠ Not an open destination. Anyone not from Tumbatu — including Zanzibaris — needs written permission from the village elders, and visits go with an approved local guide who asks for that blessing first. Do not hire a boat and turn up. The island's reputation for keeping outsiders out is earned and deliberate.
price_range: Guided cultural visit, arranged in advance
reservation: Permit + approved guide, arranged days ahead through Mkokotoni
best_time: Morning crossing on a settled tide

name: Mangapwani coral cave & slave chamber
neighborhood: West coast · about 20 km north of Stone Town
why: Two sites on the same stretch of coast, and the darkest hour on this island's road. The coral cave is natural — a cavern inside the reef limestone with a freshwater spring, which is why it could hide people. The slave chamber is man-made, cut around 1880 by Mohammed bin Nassor Al-Alwi, and it was used *after* the 1873 treaty that was supposed to have ended the trade: a holding cell for human cargo, worked until about 1905. You go down the steps into it. Zanzibar's spice wealth and this room are the same story, and a food guide that skips it is lying by omission.
hook: A freshwater cave and, a kilometre away, a cut stone cell used for twenty years after abolition.
signature: The steps down into the chamber
verdict: Go, and take a guide who will tell it properly. This is the counterweight to every clove-scented spice tour on the island.
caveat: Sombre, unlit and low-ceilinged. Entry around US$5 for a foreign adult; small notes. Not a place for a casual half hour between beaches.
reservation: None; a guide is worth it
best_time: Morning, on the way to or from Stone Town

name: Stone Town
neighborhood: South-west · about 56 km from Kendwa, roughly 1 h 15 by road
hours: Always; the night market from about 18:00
why: The other half of this island and the reason the north tip has the food it has. Everything Swahili-Arab-Indian on a Nungwi menu was assembled here first, in a port that ran the western Indian Ocean. Give it a full day, not an afternoon: the market at Darajani in the morning, the slave-market memorial and the cathedral, then the Forodhani night market at dusk and dinner on a rooftop.
hook: Fifty-six kilometres and one civilisation away from the sunbed.
signature: Darajani in the morning, Forodhani at dusk, a rooftop after dark
verdict: A full day or don't bother. The drive each way eats three hours of daylight.
caveat: Do not attempt it as a half-day from Kendwa; the road is slow and you will see a car park and a curio shop.
price_range: Transfer roughly US$50–70 each way by private car; shared transfers less
reservation: Arrange the car the day before
best_time: Leave Kendwa by 08:00; be at Forodhani by 18:00

name: Forodhani Gardens night market
neighborhood: Stone Town · the seafront, in front of the Old Fort
why: The seafront gardens turn into an open-air night market at sunset and it is the single best concentration of Zanzibari street food anywhere. The gardens were laid out in 1936 for Sultan Khalifa's silver jubilee — they were the Jubilee Gardens until the 1964 revolution — and were rebuilt in 2009 by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture. 'Forodhani' means customs, which is what stood here. Eat the Zanzibar pizza and the urojo; ignore the seafood platters glistening under lights for four hours.
hook: A customs house that became a jubilee garden that became the island's night kitchen.
signature: A Zanzibar pizza cooked to order and a cup of urojo
verdict: Go for the things cooked in front of you and nothing else — that rule turns a tourist trap into the best street food on the island.
caveat: ⚠ Never take from a tray that has been sitting out. Agree the price before it is made — overcharging visitors is routine here. Cash, small notes.

name: Emerson Spice Rooftop Tea House
neighborhood: Stone Town · Tharia Street, Mkunazini
hours: Lunch 12:30–16:00 daily · dinner from 18:00, first course served 19:00
why: The best dinner on the island and the reason to stay a night in Stone Town rather than drive back. A seafood tasting menu, US$55, one sitting a night, served on a rooftop above the old town with the call to prayer coming up from four directions and the sun going into the sea. Sundowners from six, food at seven. Reservations are required and it is not a formality.
hook: One sitting a night, US$55, on a roof above the old town.
signature: The seafood tasting menu at 19:00, with the rooftop to yourself beforehand
verdict: The island's best table by a distance — and the only one where the room, the hour and the cooking are all doing the same thing.
caveat: Reservation required, in advance. Check the day: the rooftop has carried scheduled closures in past seasons.

neighborhood: Stone Town · 236 Hurumzi Street, Kiponda
hours: Lunch 12:00–16:00 · dinner, single seating at 19:00, guests welcomed from 18:00
why: The other Emerson roof, and the more theatrical of the two: 360-degree views over the old town, Swahili floor seating on Persian rugs, and live taarab — the Zanzibari orchestral song form that is the island's own music, not a folklore act. US$45 for three courses, one seating, deposit required.
hook: Floor cushions, 360 degrees of rooftops, and live taarab at seven.
signature: Dinner cross-legged on the roof with the taarab going
verdict: Choose this one for the music and the room; choose Emerson Spice for the food.
caveat: Floor seating on rugs — not for every back. Deposit required to confirm.

name: Lukmaan Restaurant
neighborhood: Stone Town · New Mkunazini Road
why: The canteen where Stone Town itself eats: a counter of trays, you point, they plate, you sit at a shared table. Biryani, pilau, urojo, fish in coconut, cassava, spinach, chutneys — the whole Zanzibari repertoire at once, at a fraction of any rooftop. If you eat one meal in Stone Town and want to learn something, eat this one.
hook: Point at the trays. The whole Zanzibari repertoire, at the price the town pays.
signature: A tray of four or five things chosen at the counter, with urojo alongside
verdict: The single most educational plate on the island, and it costs almost nothing.
caveat: No alcohol, shared tables, and it empties fast at Friday lunch. Cash.

name: Darajani Market
neighborhood: Stone Town · Market Street
hours: From dawn; the fish hall is finished by late morning
why: Stone Town's market, and the place where the whole spice-island economy becomes ordinary again: cloves and cardamom sold by the scoop next to plastic buckets, a fish hall at the back with the morning's catch on stone slabs, and the coffee men with brass kettles at the edges. If you are provisioning anything, this is the deepest inventory on the island.
hook: Where the spice island stops being a brochure and becomes a scoop and a scale.
signature: Cloves bought loose by weight, and a cup of kahawa chungu at the market edge
verdict: The best provisioning stop on Unguja and the only place to buy spice at a real price.
caveat: Crowded, hot, and the fish hall is not for the squeamish. Buy spice loose by weight, never in a printed gift box — the box costs more than the cloves.

name: Mnemba Atoll
neighborhood: Offshore, north-east · reached from Nungwi or Matemwe
hours: Day trips from the north tip
why: The island is private and you cannot land on it; the water around it is a marine conservation area and it is the best snorkelling and easiest good diving reachable from the north tip. There is a US$10 per-person conservation fee. &Beyond, which runs the island lodge, operates a marine programme there — Oceans Without Borders, with Wild Impact — including a coral-reef restoration project. Turtles are common and seen wild, which is the honest alternative to a turtle pond.
hook: A private island you cannot land on, ringed by the best water on this coast.
signature: A drift over the atoll edge with green turtles below you
verdict: The place to see turtles honestly — wild, unfed and not in a pond.
caveat: ⚠ You cannot land on the island: it is private, and boats that promise a beach landing are selling you something they cannot deliver. The US$10 conservation fee is on top of the trip price.
price_range: Dive or snorkel trip + US$10 per-person conservation fee
reservation: Through any north-tip dive centre, day before
best_time: Early departure, before the wind gets up

name: Leven Bank
neighborhood: Offshore, north · the Pemba Channel
why: A submerged reef about two nautical miles long, out in the Pemba Channel north of the island, with walls dropping past 160 metres. Big water, big fish, and currents that decide whether the day happens at all: it can only be dived on certain tides, and every north-tip dive centre will tell you the same thing about who should be on the boat. This is the north tip's serious dive and the reason experienced divers come here rather than to the east coast.
hook: Two miles of submerged reef in open channel, divable only on the right tide.
signature: The drop past the shoulder into the channel current
verdict: The best dive reachable from this beach, and the one most likely to be cancelled — take the cancellation as professionalism, not bad luck.
caveat: ⚠ Experienced divers only, strong current, and genuinely tide-gated. Do not make it your first dive of a trip. The name most likely honours HMS Leven, which surveyed this coast in the 1820s — but we could not confirm the naming from a primary source, so we are not asserting it.
reservation: Book on a tide, not on a date
hot_this_month: Feeding hard right now: the kusi is pushing nutrient-rich water across the bank. Still tide-gated.

name: Kizimbani spice plantation
neighborhood: Central Unguja · inland from Stone Town, on the Kendwa road
hours: Daytime tours, roughly half a day including transfer
why: One of the oldest of the island's spice estates and the one to choose if you want the agriculture rather than the gift shop. This is where the whole Zanzibar story is grown: Sultan Said moved his capital here from Muscat around 1840 and decreed three clove trees planted for every coconut palm, and by the end of the nineteenth century this archipelago was producing something close to nine-tenths of the world's cloves. Kizimbani lets you watch cloves being picked and dried, and taste vanilla, nutmeg, cinnamon and pepper off the plant.
hook: Where the three-trees-to-one-palm decree of the 1840s is still standing up as agriculture.
signature: A clove picked green off the tree and rolled between your fingers
verdict: The right spice farm if you actually cook — you leave knowing what an unopened flower bud smells like, which no jar will teach you.
caveat: Every driver has a spice farm they are paid to take you to. Name Kizimbani and hold to it. Harvest activity peaks in the dry seasons — June to October and December to February.

name: The Old Fort (Ngome Kongwe)
neighborhood: Stone Town · seafront, beside Forodhani
hours: Daytime; courtyard events in the evening
why: The Omani fort on the seafront, built over the site of the earlier Portuguese chapel, and now a courtyard of craft stalls and an amphitheatre. It stands immediately beside Forodhani, so the night-market walk starts here by default.
hook: An Omani fort on a Portuguese footprint, with the night market at its gate.
verdict: Twenty minutes, free, and it orients the whole seafront.
caveat: The stalls inside are curio stalls; the building is the point.

name: Christ Church Cathedral & the slave-market memorial
neighborhood: Stone Town · Mkunazini
why: The Anglican cathedral was built on the site of the last open slave market in Zanzibar, and the altar is said to stand where the whipping post stood. The underground holding chambers survive beneath the adjacent buildings. Together with Mangapwani this is the honest half of the spice-island story, and it is a short walk from the restaurant you will eat in afterwards.
hook: An altar where the whipping post stood, and the holding chambers still underneath.
verdict: Non-optional if you are going to enjoy the cloves.
caveat: Entry fee; the chambers are low, dark and deliberately hard.

name: House of Wonders (Beit el-Ajaib)
neighborhood: Stone Town · seafront
hours: Closed to the public — exterior only
why: The sultan's palace on the seafront, once the tallest building in East Africa and the first in Zanzibar with electricity and a lift. Part of it collapsed in 2020 and it has been under restoration since; you cannot go in. It matters to this guide for one reason: it housed the great Dhow Cultures exhibition, including *Shungwaya*, the 2003 reconstruction of a sewn mtepe — the last of a two-thousand-year-old shipbuilding tradition. When the roof came down the mtepe was moved outdoors and has been weathering ever since.
hook: The building that held the last sewn ship — and lost its roof in 2020.
verdict: Closed, and worth walking past anyway: it is the physical state of this island's maritime memory.
caveat: ⚠ Closed to the public. Anyone offering you a tour inside is not selling what they say they are.

name: Freddie Mercury House
neighborhood: Stone Town · Kenyatta Road, Shangani
why: Farrokh Bulsara was born in Zanzibar in 1946 to a Parsi family from Gujarat; the house on Kenyatta Road is now a small museum. Worth twenty minutes for what it says about this island rather than about Queen: a Persian-Indian family, a British protectorate, a boy sent to school in Bombay, a family that left at the 1964 revolution. That is a Zanzibari biography, and it is the same one the food has.
hook: A Parsi boy from Gujarat born on a British-protected Omani island — a Zanzibari biography with a famous ending.
verdict: Twenty minutes and a small fee; go for the migration story, not the memorabilia.
caveat: Small, and priced as a novelty. Do not build a morning around it.

name: Smiles Beach Hotel
neighborhood: Nungwi · Mkunguni side
why: A small independent hotel with a kitchen open to walk-ins — useful as a quieter alternative when the beach strip is at full volume.
hook: Small, independent and quiet, with a kitchen that will feed you anyway.
verdict: A calm table when the strip is not.
caveat: Limited menu out of season.

hook: Cottages in a garden, and the shade to sit out the worst of the afternoon.
verdict: Pleasant and quiet; a shade address rather than a food one.

name: Nungwi village shops & the provisioning line
neighborhood: Nungwi · inland of the beach
hours: Daylight into early evening; Friday prayers close things around midday
why: Practical reality for anyone cooking: there is no proper supermarket at the north tip. What there is, is a line of small dukas through the village selling rice, flour, oil, UHT milk, eggs, onions, tomatoes, limes, chillies, charcoal and cold drinks — plus fruit sellers with mango, papaya, passion fruit and the small sweet island bananas. Fish comes off the landing, not out of a chiller. Anything else — wine, cheese, butter, decent coffee, spice in bulk — is a Stone Town run.
hook: No supermarket, a hundred dukas, and everything cold coming out of the sea.
verdict: Perfectly adequate for cooking simply and completely inadequate for cooking Europeanly. Plan accordingly.
caveat: ⚠ Cold chain is the constraint: buy fish at the landing and cook it the same day. Cash, small notes. Friday around midday the village closes for prayers.

galley: Fish and octopus off the Nungwi landing at dawn, or Mkokotoni for better prices and range. Ice is the bottleneck: buy it where you buy the fish and use it that day. Everything imported is a Stone Town run — budget three hours each way.
hot_this_month: Passion fruit now, pineapple from September, at the village fruit sellers.

name: Combo 1990
neighborhood: Nungwi · the middle of the village, off the beach
why: Seven tables with cushioned couches in the middle of Nungwi village, and the single most instructive order on the north tip: the Swahili tapas, where you choose five different local dishes from the day's pots and they arrive together with rice or ugali and chapati. There is a vegetarian version. Reviews here do not talk about the food first — they talk about Joy, who runs the room, which tells you what kind of place it is.
hook: Five dishes off the day's pots, seven tables, and Joy running the room.
person: Joy — named in review after review before the food is
signature: The Swahili tapas — five local dishes, rice or ugali, chapati

name: The dhow-building course, Nungwi
neighborhood: Nungwi · in the working boatyards on the beach
hours: Arranged in advance; daytime, alongside the yard's own working hours
why: The one thing on this cape that clears the whole bar. Zanzibar's boatbuilding capital teaches its craft to outsiders in the yard itself — not a demonstration laid on beside a hotel, but the shipwrights' own workplace, with their own tools and their own timber. Placements run through World Unite!, whose own course page names the teacher: Mr. Mponda, who learned the trade from his father in a family that has built dhows for generations, and who gives two hours of instruction a day in English while you assist the crew the rest of the time. You work on hulls that are actually being built and will actually go to sea.

name: Mwani Zanzibar
neighborhood: Paje · east coast, about 1 h 30 from Kendwa
hours: Morning visits, timed to low tide
why: A former women's seaweed-growers' cooperative that became a cosmetics maker, working out of a coconut-thatched production hut a few steps from Paje beach. The Mwani Mamas handcraft soaps, scrubs and butters from the seaweed they used to only farm, with herbs and spices from the centre's own gardens. The economics are the story: staff hold permanent contracts with salary, holiday and sick pay, and the lowest-paid is on thirty per cent above minimum wage — against an island average near US$35 a month for raw seaweed farming. A morning visit goes out on the low tide to meet the growers and then into the workshop.
hook: The women who used to only farm the seaweed now make the product — and hold the contracts.
person: The Mwani Mamas, salaried and on permanent contracts
signature: Low tide with the growers, then the workshop where it becomes soap
verdict: The most honest place on this island to spend money on a souvenir, because you can see exactly whose wage it becomes.
caveat: ⚠ ET bar, honestly: this is a **guided visit to a working production floor, not an enrolment**. You watch and you buy; you do not learn the craft as a student. It clears at-the-source and dedicated-to-the-craft, and it fails open-enrolment. Listed for what it is. Also 1 h 30 from Kendwa on the far coast — a day, not a detour.

It is a teaching operation rather than a restaurant putting on a demonstration, it is run in and by a Zanzibari village, and you can book it as an outsider. If you want to actually learn to build mchuzi wa nazi rather than be shown it, this is the closest thing on the island to a school.
